title: Inventory and Aftermath
premise: Ansel Oyelaran has spent fifteen years as the night librarian of a sleepless city, hiding behind a professional smile and a surname he shortened to escape his family's political legacy. At his estranged father's funeral, a stranger addresses the mourners by 'Oyelaran-Adeyemi,' a name erased from all records after a scandal Ansel barely remembers, and claims his father left him an inventory: a ledger of everyone the family's power broke. As city officials close in to bury the ledger and the truth with it, Ansel must decide whether invisibility is safety or complicity. He ends by reading the names aloud at dawn in the library's reading room, choosing love—his partner Ilsa, who never knew his real name—over the duty of silence, knowing it will cost him everything but himself.
about_author: Dominic Sandoval is the pen name of a former night-shift archivist who spent a decade cataloguing the papers of disgraced public figures before turning to fiction. He writes about people who mistake disappearance for peace.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. A night shift at the Halcyon Branch Library: patrons who cannot sleep, a colleague who tries too hard to befriend him, and Ilsa, the transit nurse he loves but keeps at arm's length. We see his perfected deflections. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as competence.

chapters.title: Notice of Service
chapters.summary: Ansel receives word that his father, Senator Emeka Oyelaran, has died. He hasn't spoken to him in twelve years. Ilsa offers to come; he refuses without explaining why there's nothing to explain. POV: Ansel. Beat: grief arriving as paperwork.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: At the funeral, among strangers and cameras, an old woman grips Ansel's arm and says, 'You're an Oyelaran-Adeyemi.' The hyphenated name detonates something in him; his mother flinches across the room. POV: Ansel. Beat: the past refusing to stay buried.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Second Row
chapters.summary: The woman, Mrs. Adebanke Fashola, slips him a key and an address before vanishing. She says his father 'kept accounts.' Ansel's brother Tunde warns him to walk away—the family name is finally clean, don't dig. POV: Ansel. Beat: temptation wrapped in obligation.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Keeps
chapters.summary: In a storage unit, Ansel finds the inventory: decades of payments, favors, and ruined lives recorded in his father's hand, including one entry dated the year of the scandal that split the family. POV: Ansel, with ledger excerpts. Beat: horror of inheritance.

chapters.title: Ilsa, at Four in the Morning
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. She reads Ansel's sleeplessness like a chart she can't treat. Their intimacy is real but walled; she names it gently over shared coffee. He almost tells her everything and doesn't. Beat: love pressing against the wall of secrecy.

chapters.title: The City That Sleeps Less
chapters.summary: Ansel researches the scandal: the Adeyemi dam project, the flooded valley, the renamed survivors. The library's own archives hold the sanitized version. He realizes his father kept the true record as leverage—or penance. POV: Ansel. Beat: the scale of the lie becomes personal.

chapters.title: Tunde's Bargain
chapters.summary: Tunde reveals he already knows about the ledger; a city fixer named Corver offered him money and a future for its destruction. Tunde wants Ansel to hand it over for the family's sake. POV: Tunde. Beat: brotherhood as negotiation.

chapters.title: Mrs. Fashola's Testimony
chapters.summary: Ansel finds Adebanke, a survivor of the flooded valley. She tells him why his father sent her the key: guilt, or insurance, or both. She asks not for justice but for the names to be said once, aloud. POV: alternating Ansel/Adebanke. Beat: witness as burden.

chapters.title: Corver Visits the Library
chapters.summary: The fixer appears at the Halcyon desk, courteous, offering Ansel a promotion-shaped bribe and a threat-shaped smile. Ansel stalls. His supervisor notices the visit and grows nervous. POV: Ansel. Beat: power showing its polite face.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Small Cowardices
chapters.summary: Ansel audits his own life the way his father audited others: every silence, every shortcut, the way he let Ilsa believe he had no family history worth telling. POV: Ansel. Beat: turning the ledger inward.

chapters.title: Ilsa Asks the Real Question
chapters.summary: Ilsa confronts him—not about the ledger, which she's guessed exists, but about whether he trusts her with his worst self. He gives her half the truth. She stays anyway, which frightens him more than leaving would. POV: Ilsa. Beat: love demanding honesty, receiving partial payment.

chapters.title: The Storage Unit Is Empty
chapters.summary: Someone got there first. Ansel traces the break-in to a private security firm contracted by the city. Panic: the only copies are in his memory and one photograph he took of a single page—his mother's name is on it. POV: Ansel. Beat: rising dread.

chapters.title: His Mother's Entry
chapters.summary: Ansel confronts his mother, Ngozi, who admits she helped bury the scandal to protect her sons—and that the entry naming her records what she did to keep quiet. She begs him to let the dead rest. POV: Ngozi. Beat: complicity inherited from both sides.

chapters.title: Adebanke's Deadline
chapters.summary: Adebanke is dying; the anniversary commemoration of the flood is in nine days. If the names aren't read publicly then, the last witnesses will be gone. Ansel commits, then immediately doubts. POV: Ansel. Beat: the clock starts.

chapters.title: Tunde Chooses
chapters.summary: Tunde takes Corver's money—but secretly passes Ansel the firm's surveillance schedule, unable to fully betray either side. The brothers reconcile partially, imperfectly. POV: Tunde. Beat: loyalty fractured but not broken.

chapters.title: Reconstructing the Ledger
chapters.summary: In the library after hours, Ansel, Ilsa, and Adebanke rebuild the inventory from memory, archives, and the photographed page. Ilsa finally learns the full truth and stays. POV: ensemble, anchored by Ansel. Beat: love against duty resolved into partnership.

chapters.title: Corver's Last Offer
chapters.summary: Cornered, Ansel meets Corver, who reveals the ledger was always meant for him—his father's final test or final cruelty. The offer now includes erasure of Ansel's own complicity. POV: Ansel. Beat: the climax's threshold; power offers him a place inside it.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.summary: Ansel prepares the reading room, arranges chairs, drafts the speech he may never finish. He visits his father's grave and speaks to it honestly for the first time. Quiet, devastating chapter. POV: Ansel. Beat: farewell as preparation.

chapters.title: Reading the Names
chapters.summary: At the flood anniversary, officials attempt to shut the event down; Ansel opens the library instead and begins reading the ledger aloud, name by name, as citizens arrive and take turns continuing when his voice fails. POV: Ansel. Beat: climax—truth spoken out loud, communally.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Consequences land: Ansel loses his position, faces investigation, gains unexpected allies. Tunde testifies. His mother visits the library as a patron, saying nothing, staying an hour. POV: shifting vignettes. Beat: cost accounted, dignity intact.

chapters.title: Inventory, Revised
chapters.summary: Months later, Ansel works days at a smaller branch, unhidden, using his full name on the door placard. With Ilsa, he begins writing the valley's true history. The last line mirrors the first: a stranger asks him a question, and this time he answers. POV: Ansel. Beat: resolution—identity chosen, love kept, silence ended.
